summary: We developed AgroNASA Spain, an interactive Python and Streamlit web application that generates tailored 3-year crop rotation plans across Spain’s 17 autonomous communities. The platform integrates 24 years of NASA POWER Earth observation data (2001–2024)—including temperature, precipitation, root-zone soil moisture, and decadal climate trends—with user-defined plot conditions such as soil type, irrigation access, organic matter, and strategic priorities. To address agricultural climate adaptation, our weighted scoring engine evaluates 13 crops across drought tolerance, water demand, profitability, and nitrogen fixation while preventing consecutive botanical families to break pest cycles. Crucially, if NASA records show declining rainfall trends, the model automatically adjusts local water availability downward to recommend resilient species. This tool is important because it translates complex satellite climate records into practical, field-level decisions, helping farmers conserve water, naturally regenerate soil nitrogen, and maintain productivity amid intensifying droughts.
details:
How It Works:

AgroNASA Spain is an interactive web application that generates personalized 3-year crop rotation plans across Spain’s 17 autonomous communities. First, an automated data-collection script queries the NASA POWER Agroclimatology API to retrieve 24 years of monthly satellite and weather records (2001–2024) for each region, specifically 2-meter air temperature (T2M), bias-corrected precipitation (PRECTOTCORR), and root-zone soil wetness (GWETROOT). The script computes long-term climate averages as well as decadal trends comparing 2015–2024 against 2001–2010. Next, inside the web interface, users select their autonomous community and enter their plot conditions: soil texture (loam, sandy, or clay), water availability (rainfed or irrigated), organic matter level, and primary management goal (saving water, regenerating soil, or maximizing profit). Our decision engine then evaluates 13 crops using a weighted scoring formula that balances water demand, drought resistance, economic return, nitrogen fixation, and soil compatibility. Crucially, if NASA records show a negative rainfall trend in that region, the model automatically reduces effective precipitation to reflect drier conditions. It also enforces strict agronomic rules—such as excluding irrigation-dependent crops from dry rainfed plots, starting with a cover crop when soil organic matter is low, and never repeating the same botanical family in consecutive years—before outputting the 3-year plan alongside climate risk alerts and sustainability indicators for water consumption, nitrogen balance, and soil health.

Benefits and Intended Impact:

Spain faces severe climate vulnerability, with NASA POWER data highlighting significant warming and sharp multi-decade rainfall declines in regions such as Andalusia and the Canary Islands. AgroNASA Spain bridges the gap between raw Earth observation data and practical field decisions without requiring technical expertise from the user. By pairing climate-resilient crops with nitrogen-fixing legumes (such as chickpeas, lentils, peas, fava beans, and vetch) and rotating botanical families (Poaceae, Fabaceae, Asteraceae, and Brassicaceae), the tool helps farmers reduce synthetic fertilizer expenses, naturally break pest and disease cycles, and prevent crop failure. Our intended impact is to empower small and medium-sized farmers to adapt to intensifying droughts, conserve scarce water resources, restore degraded soils, and maintain long-term economic viability.

Tools, Languages, and Software Used:

We built the entire project in Python 3. We used Streamlit to develop the interactive web interface, Plotly (plotly.graph_objects) to render a custom interactive polygon map of Spain’s autonomous communities, and Python’s standard libraries (urllib.request, json, os, and time) to fetch, process, and cache climate data from the NASA POWER API. Development and testing were carried out on standard personal computers.

What Makes It Creative:

Rather than simply displaying static weather dashboards or recommending a single crop in isolation, our project integrates retrospective decadal satellite trends directly into a multi-year agronomic rotation algorithm. By dynamically discounting water availability whenever historical NASA rainfall trends are negative, the model links past climate shifts to forward-looking farm planning. In addition, building a lightweight vector map directly from custom coordinate polygons in Plotly and including an offline fallback climate dataset keeps the application fast, dependency-light, and reliable even in rural areas with limited internet connectivity.

Factors Our Team Considered:

Our team accounted for four main dimensions when designing the system: climatic trends and extremes (24-year averages, decadal precipitation shifts, water deficits below 350 mm, waterlogging risks above 900 mm, and heat stress above 18 °C), agronomic sustainability (soil texture matching, soil organic matter, biological nitrogen fixation versus depletion, and botanical family rotation to curb soil-borne pathogens), farm resource trade-offs (rainfed versus irrigated plots and competing economic or environmental priorities), and accessibility for non-technical end users.
